name: Hana Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm one of eleven worker-members at Ampersand, an electrical co-op. A co-op means we own the firm together and vote on the big decisions. Most of my week is wiring heat pumps and smart controls into houses, plus the odd café or hair salon that needs a new board. I start the day with an AI assistant on my phone that's already sorted my route, pulled the wiring diagrams for the heat pump model, and flagged which customer pays late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You use AI every day. What does that look like on an actual job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Say I'm fault-finding a heat pump that keeps tripping. I photograph the board, describe the symptoms, and the assistant gives me three likely causes in order, and it's right maybe two times in three. I still test everything myself, the meter doesn't lie. I live with my partner Jo, who works in a library, and we rent a flat above a bakery, so I wake up to bread smell, which is the best perk in the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the tools are handy and that's all they are. At the co-op meeting I'd say we keep using what saves us time and stop paying for the rest. Online I'd probably post that the real story was always heat pumps, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means not much changes. Heat pump work is booming because of the grants, we've got a waiting list, and Jo and I have around five months saved. I'm comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant for routes and fault-finding, because it already saves me about an hour a day. I'd push at the co-op to buy the better quoting software. And I'd keep paying into the fund to buy my full member share, which I finish next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little disappointed, I like new toys, but my work's solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does buying your full member share mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I put in 4,000 over two years and get a full vote and a share of any surplus. I'm about 3,000 in. Owning a share in the co-op is the closest thing I'll have to owning a business without owning it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your situation that worries you, even with nothing changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The heat pump grants. If a new government cuts them, our waiting list halves overnight. But we'd go back to rewires and boards, there's always work for a decent electrician round here.

say: I'd say the **tools are handy** and nothing more, so keep the useful ones.
Online I'd say the real story was always **heat pumps**, not robots.
think: Heat pump work is **booming**, and we have about **five months** saved.
The only cloud is a future government cutting **heat pump grants**.
do: Keep using the **AI assistant** for routes and fault-finding every day.
Push the co-op to buy better **quoting software**.
Finish paying the **4,000 member share** next year.
feel: **Calm**, with a small **disappointment** because she likes new tools.
S0.quote: Owning a share in the co-op is the closest thing I'll have to owning a business without owning it alone.
fieldNote: Already uses AI daily and sees it as a **time-saver**, not a threat.
The **co-op share** gives her a stake and a sense of control.
Her only real risk is **policy**: grants for heat pumps.

steps.text: Keep wiring heat pumps and smart controls for the co-op
Push the co-op to buy better quoting software
Finish paying the 4,000 co-op member share next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where co-ops shine, because the gains stay with the people doing the work. At the co-op meeting I'd propose we bring in AI for quoting and booking and use the time saved to take on two more apprentices. Online I'd argue for rules so big firms have to share gains the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. My job is hands-on and I already use the tools, so I'd be ahead. The part I'd watch is Rashida, who does our office work, because her tasks are on the card, so we'd need to retrain her into estimating or site supervision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lead the switch at Ampersand: trial an AI quoting and booking system in the first three months, then roll it out. I'd take a short course on smart-building controls, which is where I think the new work is. And I'd vote to keep everyone on, with Rashida moving into supervising jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. The kind of change I'd want to be steering, not dodging.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd vote to keep Rashida on. What if the numbers didn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd cut hours across the board before we cut a person, that's the whole point of a co-op. I'd take a four-day week. Rashida's a friend, and I'd rather earn a bit less than sit across the table from a friend at a co-op meeting where we vote her out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about this make you nervous?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Other firms using AI to underbid us on price. If a big contractor quotes in ten seconds and undercuts us by twenty percent, we'll feel it. That's why I'd want us faster too.

I'd argue for rules making big firms **share the gains** with staff.
think: My **hands-on job** is safe and I already use the tools, so I'm ahead.

feel: **Calm** and a little **excited** to be steering the change.

fieldNote: Sees the co-op as a **model** for sharing AI gains fairly.

steps.text: Trial an AI quoting and booking system at the co-op

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make the robots and the AI publicly owned, or at least co-owned, so the gains don't vanish into three companies. I'd say it at the co-op, in the union and online. And I'd say it loudly, because two years isn't long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it hits our estimating and design work in 2028, which is fine, we'd automate it. The hard part is 2031, when robots can do what I do with my hands. I'd be 32, and I'd need to be on the side that owns or runs the robots, not the side that gets replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away, I'd push Ampersand to start saving for its own robots, so we own the kit instead of renting labour from some giant firm. I'd learn everything I can about how they're programmed and maintained. And I'd put an extra 200 a month aside, because I'm not daft, the co-op could still go under.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. The kind of nervous that gets you out of bed early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a small co-op can't afford robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd team up with other co-ops, there are four in the region. A shared robot pool for co-ops would work like farmers sharing a combine harvester. If we can't do that, we're finished, and I'd be looking for work like everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jo that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jo that the library job might actually outlast mine, which is funny. And I'd say we should keep the rent low and not buy anything for a year. Jo would make tea and ask if we should move to the country, as always.

say: I'd call for robots and AI to be **publicly or co-owned**.
I'd say it **loudly** in the co-op, the union and online, because time is short.
think: Estimating goes in **2028**, which is fine; **robots in 2031** are the real threat.
I need to be on the side that **owns the robots**, not the replaced side.
do: Push Ampersand to save for **its own robots**.
Learn how the **robots are programmed** and maintained.
Save an extra **200 a month** in case the co-op fails.
feel: **Anxious** but with a plan, the nerves that get her up **early**.
S2.quote: A shared robot pool for co-ops would work like farmers sharing a combine harvester.
fieldNote: Even an early adopter turns **anxious** when robots arrive in five years.
Her answer is **ownership**: the co-op must own the robots.
Admits the co-op **could fail**, and saves against it.

steps.text: Push the co-op to start a fund for its own robots
Learn how building robots are programmed and maintained

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for co-ops and councils to get organised, if they start now. I'd post about the robot-pool idea and try to get other co-ops on board. And at work I'd say let's be the first co-op in the region to own one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's tight but workable. The thinking side goes in 2031, which we'd have automated by then anyway. Robots for hands-on come around 2034, when I'm 35, and by then I'd want to be running Ampersand's robot crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd start a regional group with the other four co-ops to plan a shared robot fund. I'd take a course in robotics maintenance at the technical college, two evenings a week. Jo and I would keep renting and keep our savings growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than anxious. It's on my mind, but it feels like something I can shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big firms and the governments that let them own everything. Not the technology. A robot doesn't decide who gets paid, people do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the extra years change how you feel about your own trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit sad, honestly. I like the feel of a clean termination in a board. But I'd rather be the person who teaches a robot to do it right than the person who pretends it won't happen.

I'd recruit other co-ops to the **shared robot pool** idea online.
think: Thinking tasks go in **2031**, and we'd have **automated** them anyway.
By **2034** I'd want to be running Ampersand's **robot crew**.

Take a **robotics maintenance** course two evenings a week.

fieldNote: Blames **firms and governments**, never the technology itself.
Shows quiet **grief** for the craft, alongside eagerness to adapt.

steps.text: Start a group with four regional co-ops for a robot fund
Take a robotics maintenance course at the technical college
Plan for Ampersand to run its own robot crew by 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone being left behind. I'd argue for every trade college to start teaching robot work now. At the co-op I'd say let's plan, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 39 when robots come in 2039, with ten years of being the co-op's tech person behind me. I think I'd be in a good spot. My bigger worry would be whether Jo and I can afford to buy somewhere before prices jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with heat pumps, finish my member share, and slowly build the co-op's tech side. Maybe a robotics course in a few years, not right away. And we'd start looking for a small house with a garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's far off, I'm adaptable, and I'd have a stake in the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a school leaver thinking about being an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say do it, and learn the software too. The trade will need people who understand both the wiring and the robots for a good while. A new electrician shouldn't expect to do the same job at 50 that they did at 20.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could make this picture go badly for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the robot makers only lease to big contractors and freeze small firms out. Then we'd be competing with one hand tied. That's the one thing I'd watch.

say: I'd say with **ten years**, nobody has an **excuse** for being left behind.
I'd argue every **trade college** should start teaching robot work now.
think: By **2039** I'd be 39 with a decade as the co-op's **tech person**.
My bigger worry would be **house prices**, not my job.
do: Carry on wiring **heat pumps** and finish the member share.
Build up the co-op's **tech side** gradually.
Start looking for a **small house** with Jo.
feel: **Calm**, because she is adaptable and owns a **stake** in the firm.
S4.quote: A new electrician shouldn't expect to do the same job at 50 that they did at 20.
fieldNote: Ten years puts her in a **strong spot** as the co-op's tech lead.
Her one fear is robot makers **freezing out small firms**.
Advice to school leavers: learn **wiring and software** together.

steps.text: Keep wiring heat pumps and smart controls

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because small firms like ours wouldn't have time to get the money together for our own robots. What would help is public loans or grants for co-ops and small firms to own the kit, not just rent it from the giants. And free robot training at every trade college.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people who owns the robots. That's the whole question for me. Whether it's good or bad comes down to that.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be the person who teaches a robot to do it right than the person who pretends it won't happen.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old co-op electrician** wiring heat pumps and smart controls.
She uses **AI daily** for routes, diagrams and fault-finding, and still trusts her meter first.
She sees **ownership** as the key question: who owns the robots and AI.
Fast AGI makes her **anxious**; slower versions leave her uneasy or calm.
She plans to run the co-op's **robot crew** and pushes a shared regional robot fund.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because small co-ops couldn't raise money for their own robots in time.
whatWouldHelp: **Public loans** for co-ops and small firms to own robots.
Free **robot training** at every trade college.
